title: Mother of God (Council of Ephesus, 431)
hook: the crowds in Ephesus cheered when the council called Mary God-bearer, a claim about who Jesus is

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Immaculate Conception: Mary's own beginning, kept free of original sin. Your line was prepared from the start.

Summer, 431, in the city of Ephesus, on the coast of what's now Turkey. Around two hundred bishops have gathered in a church dedicated to Mary, and the whole city is waiting outside. They've been arguing for months about one word, a word ordinary people used in their prayers. Late in the evening the decision comes out, and the crowd goes wild. People light torches and walk the bishops back to their lodgings, singing, with incense burning in the streets. All over a title for a mother that was really a claim about her son.
screen: `EPHESUS, 431.` → `TWO HUNDRED BISHOPS, ONE WORD.` → `TORCHES IN THE STREETS.`

segments.voice: Theotokos. Greek: theos, God, and tokos, giving birth. God-bearer, or in English, Mother of God. Christians had been calling Mary this for a long time. But Nestorius, the archbishop of Constantinople, was uneasy. Surely, he said, Mary gave birth to the human Jesus, not to God. Better to call her Christ-bearer. It sounds careful. But Cyril, the bishop of Alexandria, argued that it led somewhere dangerous: splitting Jesus into two, a man who was born and a God who was not. The council sided with Cyril. Its teaching: Jesus isn't two people sharing a body. He's one person, truly God and truly human. So the one Mary carried and nursed and taught to walk is God the Son, and she is truly the mother of God. The title protects the truth about Jesus first. It doesn't mean Mary is older than God, or the source of God. For the council, it means the baby in her arms was God made man. Catholics hear the idea already in Elizabeth's greeting, in the Douay-Rheims: "And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?" They say the title in every Hail Mary: "Holy Mary, Mother of God, pray for us sinners, now and at the hour of our death. Amen." And the Church begins every new year with it: January first is the Solemnity of Mary, the Mother of God. Orthodox Christians use the Greek word itself in their liturgy.
screen: `THEOS AND TOKOS: GOD-BEARER.` · `NOT JUST CHRIST-BEARER.` · `ONE PERSON, GOD AND MAN.` · `JANUARY FIRST, EVERY YEAR.` · then, large: `THE MOTHER OF MY LORD.`

segments.voice: If you pray, say the Hail Mary once, so slowly that each phrase gets a breath of its own, and when you reach Mother of God, pause and let the claim land: the one she held, Catholics say, was God. If you don't pray, just hear the words in your mind and notice what they're claiming. Either way, finish in the quiet, with no rush.
Theotokos. Greek for God-bearer: Mary, Mother of God, a title that is first of all a claim about who her son is. Today's word.
Your line: a claim about her son. The title is for Mary; the point is Jesus. Day eighty, done.

howItsDone: Catholics call Mary Mother of God in every Hail Mary and celebrate the Solemnity of Mary, Mother of God, on 1 January; Orthodox Christians call her Theotokos throughout their liturgy.

chat.says: How can Mary be the Mother of God? Wasn't God there before her?
options: It's about her son: Jesus is one person, truly God and human, so she bore God.
It means Mary is the source of God, somehow older even than the Son.
It's just an honorary title for her, unrelated to who Jesus really is.
chat.meaning: Ephesus taught that Jesus is one person, truly God and truly human. So the baby Mary carried was God the Son.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 1:43 given from memory; confirm.
Council of Ephesus met June–July 431 in the Church of Mary; roughly 150–200 bishops (counts vary). Confirm 'around two hundred'.
The torchlight procession is described in a letter of Cyril of Alexandria to his church (often numbered Letter 24). Confirm the reference.
Nestorius's position summarized fairly? He preferred Christotokos; modern scholars debate how 'Nestorian' Nestorius was. Keeper may want a softer phrasing.
'Already in Christian prayer before the council': the Sub tuum praesidium (papyrus variously dated 3rd–4th century) and earlier Fathers (e.g. Alexander of Alexandria). Confirm.
Solemnity of Mary, Mother of God on 1 January. Confirm.
Hail Mary cited in its traditional English form, as on other Catholic days.
